quotes.text: A person can be morally responsible only for what he does; but what he does results from a great deal that he does not do; therefore he is not morally responsible for what he is and is not responsible for.
quotes.key_move: Compresses the argument into a three-step chain and then labels the result a paradox rather than a contradiction, refusing to resolve it.
quotes.core_assumption: The concept of responsibility carries the trouble inside it; no repair of the surrounding theory removes it.
quotes.why_characteristic: Nagel states the paradox flatly and adds that he has no solution, which is the stance that separates him from Kant and from the compatibilist reply he considers.

quotes.text: By discrediting outsiders, echo chambers leave their members overly dependent on approved inside sources for information. In epistemic bubbles, other voices are merely not heard; in echo chambers, other voices are actively undermined.
quotes.key_move: Draws the paper's governing distinction by naming two different mechanisms of exclusion, omission and active discredit.
quotes.core_assumption: Structures of exclusion differ in kind, and the difference sits in what happens to outside voices rather than in how much information gets through.
quotes.why_characteristic: The bubble/chamber contrast is the sentence the whole essay is built around, and no other assigned reading uses these terms.

quotes.text: A toy example: suppose I am a cult leader, and I have taught my followers to believe that every human except the members of our group has been infested and mind-controlled by alien ghosts from Mars.
quotes.key_move: Builds a deliberately absurd case so the mechanism can be inspected without anyone's political loyalties getting in the way.
quotes.core_assumption: A belief system can be arranged so that contradiction arrives already predicted, and prediction converts contradiction into confirmation.
quotes.why_characteristic: The Mars ghosts set up the disagreement-reinforcement mechanism, which he then connects to Begby's evidential pre-emption and to Pizzagate.

quotes.text: Bubbles restrict access to outsiders, but don’t necessarily change their credibility. Echo chambers, on the other hand, work by offering a pre-emptive discredit towards any outside sources.
quotes.key_move: Locates the difference in credence rather than access, which is what makes exposure the wrong treatment for one of the two structures.
quotes.core_assumption: Credibility assignments do more epistemic work than information flow, so a well-connected network can still be captured.
quotes.why_characteristic: "Pre-emptive discredit" is his own coinage for the manipulation of trust, and it carries the paper's argument about why exposure backfires.

quotes.text: One might be tempted to say: but just give them the real evidence! You can’t discredit neutral evidence! But this response radically underestimates the degree of trust and social processing involved in most presentations of evidence.
quotes.key_move: States the obvious fix in the reader's own voice, then blocks it by showing that evidence reaches almost everyone through chains of institutional trust.
quotes.core_assumption: There is no evidence that arrives untouched by testimony, so nothing in the epistemic toolkit is immune to a manipulation of trust.
quotes.why_characteristic: He turns his own belief in climate change into the example, tracing it through science journalists and credentialing systems rather than claiming direct access.

quotes.text: But echo chambers are the very opposite; they are reverse-mandevillian intelligences. Echo chambers are social epistemic structures which convert individually epistemically virtuous activity into collective epistemic vice.
quotes.key_move: Inverts Smart's mandevillian intelligence to shift responsibility from the believer's character onto the structure the believer was raised in.
quotes.core_assumption: Epistemic evaluation has to take the social structure as its object, since the same practices count as virtues or vices depending on where they are performed.
quotes.why_characteristic: The reverse-mandevillian label is his term, and it drives the argument that the home-schooled teenager is blameless where Cassam's Oliver is blamed.

quotes.text: Fred explains that he keeps the puppies for twenty-six weeks, and then butchers them while holding them upside-down. During their lives he performs a series of mutilations on them, such as slicing off their noses and their paws with a hot knife, all without any form of anesthesia.
quotes.source_title: Puppies, Pigs, and People: Eating Meat and Marginal Cases
quotes.key_move: Sets up the case in clinical detail so the reader condemns Fred before learning that the details match standard practice in intensive confinement facilities.
quotes.core_assumption: Moral reactions to a described practice should not change when the same practice is relabeled or moved out of sight.
quotes.why_characteristic: The basement, the twenty-six week cycle, and the unanaesthetized mutilations are the opening scene every reader of this paper remembers.

quotes.text: I expect near universal agreement with this claim (the exceptions being those who are either inhumanly callous or thinking ahead, and wish to avoid the following conclusion, to which such agreement commits them). No decent person would even contemplate torturing puppies merely to enhance a gustatory experience.
quotes.source_title: Puppies, Pigs, and People: Eating Meat and Marginal Cases
quotes.key_move: Extracts the premise everyone will grant, while warning that readers who see where it leads may refuse it for that reason alone.
quotes.core_assumption: Gustatory pleasure cannot outweigh severe suffering, and a conclusion's unpleasantness is no reason to reject a premise.
quotes.why_characteristic: The parenthetical needling of readers who are 'thinking ahead' is Norcross's tone throughout the paper.

quotes.text: A one in ten thousand chance of saving 250,000 chickens per year from excruciating lives is morally and mathematically equivalent to the certainty of saving 25 chickens per year.
quotes.source_title: Puppies, Pigs, and People: Eating Meat and Marginal Cases
quotes.key_move: Answers the causal-impotence defense with expected value, noting that the harm risked grows in exact proportion as the chance of preventing it shrinks.
quotes.core_assumption: Expected consequences, not guaranteed ones, determine what an individual consumer is responsible for.
quotes.why_characteristic: The chicken threshold arithmetic, followed by the car seat and aircraft oxygen mask comparisons, is this paper's distinctive reply to 'my choice makes no difference'.

quotes.text: Whatever kind and level of rationality is selected as justifying the attribution of superior moral status to humans will either be lacking in some humans or present in some animals.
quotes.source_title: Puppies, Pigs, and People: Eating Meat and Marginal Cases
quotes.key_move: States the argument from marginal cases as a dilemma that any rationality criterion must face before it can do the work Steinbock, Warren, and Cohen want from it.
quotes.core_assumption: A criterion of moral status must be applied to individuals, not to species averages or typical members.
quotes.why_characteristic: Norcross names 'marginal cases' in the title and builds section 5 around exactly this formulation.

quotes.text: That animals can’t be moral agents doesn’t seem to be relevant to their status as moral patients. Many, perhaps most, humans are both moral agents and patients. Most, perhaps all, animals are only moral patients.
quotes.source_title: Puppies, Pigs, and People: Eating Meat and Marginal Cases
quotes.key_move: Concedes the whole rationality claim and then denies its relevance, separating what grounds obligation from what grounds standing to be wronged.
quotes.core_assumption: Full status as a moral patient is not earned by moral agency; suffering alone grounds it.
quotes.why_characteristic: Norcross calls this the speciesist's central confusion and treats it as a deeper problem than marginal cases.

quotes.text: But I suspect that like me, you will balk at this judgment. You will think that Nora lives under Torvald’s thumb. She is the doll in a doll’s house, not a free woman.
quotes.source_title: Just Freedom: A Moral Compass for a Complex World
quotes.key_move: Refuses the verdict that noninterference delivers, inviting the reader to share the intuition that Nora is unfree.
quotes.core_assumption: Living under someone else's thumb is unfreedom even when that person never blocks a single choice.
quotes.why_characteristic: The doll's house image from Ibsen is the case the Prologue is built around.

quotes.text: To be a free person you must have the capacity to make certain central choices—choices about what religion to practice, whether to speak your mind, who to associate with, and so on—without having to seek the permission of another.
quotes.source_title: Just Freedom: A Moral Compass for a Complex World
quotes.key_move: States the positive condition for personal freedom by naming the basic liberties and the permission requirement.
quotes.core_assumption: Freedom is a status you hold in relation to others, not a running tally of choices left unblocked.
quotes.why_characteristic: The list of central choices and the phrase about seeking another's permission is how the Prologue defines a free person.

quotes.text: If you happen to be treated with indulgence and goodwill, as Nora is, then you will of course be a lot better off than if you incur the malice of the other. But even if you escape ill-treatment, you can only congratulate yourself on your good fortune, not on your freedom.
quotes.source_title: Just Freedom: A Moral Compass for a Complex World
quotes.key_move: Drives a wedge between escaping harm and being free, so that indulgence counts as luck rather than liberty.
quotes.core_assumption: Whatever you hold at another's pleasure you do not hold as a free person.
quotes.why_characteristic: Congratulating yourself on good fortune rather than freedom is the Prologue's verdict on anyone in Nora's position.

quotes.text: The eyeball test requires that people should be so resourced and protected in the basic choices of life—for short, the basic liberties—that they can look others in the eye without reason for fear or deference of the kind that a power of interference might inspire.
quotes.source_title: Just Freedom: A Moral Compass for a Complex World
quotes.key_move: Fixes a workable threshold for how much protection justice demands by making it a test anyone can apply.
quotes.core_assumption: Fear and deference in the presence of the powerful are evidence that a society has failed, not that a person is timid.
quotes.why_characteristic: The eyeball test is one of the three named tests the Prologue introduces.

quotes.text: Freedom as non-domination is not the only good in life, of course. But it is a gateway good, as we might put it: a good whose realization promises to bring the realization of other goods in its train.
quotes.source_title: Just Freedom: A Moral Compass for a Complex World
quotes.key_move: Answers the objection that one value cannot carry a whole political philosophy by arguing that securing freedom drags other goods with it.
quotes.core_assumption: Freedom can serve as the single guiding good for social justice without denying that other goods matter.
quotes.why_characteristic: The gateway good formulation is how the Prologue justifies making freedom the sole compass.

quotes.text: We differ in our beliefs, not in our values. We agree that we shouldn’t eat Grandma; we disagree about whether the cow might be Grandma.
quotes.key_move: Explains away an apparent clash of values by locating the disagreement in factual belief about what the cow is.
quotes.core_assumption: Customs differ for many reasons, so a difference in practice does not establish a difference in values.
quotes.why_characteristic: The cow-that-might-be-Grandma case is the chapter's most memorable example and belongs to Rachels's argument that cultures disagree less than they seem to.

quotes.text: Cultural Relativism holds, in effect, that societies are morally infallible—in other words, that the morals of a culture can never be wrong. But when we see that societies can and do endorse grave injustices, we see that societies, like their members, can be in need of moral improvement.
quotes.key_move: Restates the second tenet of Cultural Relativism as a claim about infallibility, then refutes it with cases of societies endorsing injustice.
quotes.core_assumption: What a society believes about morals and what is really true can come apart, so a moral code can itself be mistaken.
quotes.why_characteristic: Rachels tests each of the five tenets in turn, and this is the verdict he reaches on the tenet at the heart of the theory.

quotes.text: For an argument to be sound, its premises must all be true, and its conclusion must logically follow from them. Here, the problem is that the conclusion does not follow from the premise—that is, even if the premise is true, the conclusion might still be false.
quotes.key_move: Applies the test for soundness to the Cultural Differences Argument and diagnoses it as invalid, since its premise reports beliefs while its conclusion reports how things are.
quotes.core_assumption: A theory earns acceptance through a valid argument, and showing the argument fails leaves the conclusion unproved rather than refuted.
quotes.why_characteristic: The whole chapter turns on this diagnosis, and Rachels immediately warns that it does not show the relativist's conclusion to be false.

quotes.text: It is difficult to think of ethical principles that should hold for all people at all times. However, if we are to criticize the practice of slavery, or stoning, or genital mutilation, and if such practices are really and truly wrong, then we must appeal to principles that are not tethered to the traditions of any particular society.
quotes.key_move: Concedes how hard universal principles are to state, then argues that criticizing slavery or excision commits us to at least one principle no culture owns.
quotes.core_assumption: Moral criticism across cultures requires a standard that is not itself a local tradition, such as whether a practice helps or hurts the people affected by it.
quotes.why_characteristic: This is Rachels's answer to the third tenet, and it names the welfare standard he had already used on the Kassindja case.

quotes.text: Cultural Relativism begins with the insight that many of our practices are like this—they are only cultural products. Then it goes wrong by assuming that all of them are.
quotes.key_move: Locates the exact point of failure in a theory he has just credited, separating the true insight about conventional customs from the overgeneralization built on it.
quotes.core_assumption: A false theory can rest on a genuine insight, and the insight survives once the overgeneralization is removed.
quotes.why_characteristic: Rachels ends by saying what we can learn from Cultural Relativism, and this sentence marks the boundary between the lesson he keeps and the theory he rejects.

quotes.text: In the first, Smith stands to gain a large inheritance if anything should happen to his six-year-old cousin. One evening while the child is taking his bath, Smith sneaks into the bathroom and drowns the child, and then arranges things so that it will look like an accident.
quotes.key_move: Sets up the first half of a matched pair of cases, fixing motive and outcome so that only the killing/letting-die feature will vary.
quotes.core_assumption: Moral comparison requires cases that differ in exactly one respect, or the difference cannot be credited with the verdict.
quotes.why_characteristic: The bathtub inheritance case is the example every reader of the euthanasia paper remembers, and Rachels states it in deliberately flat, unliterary detail.

quotes.text: Now Smith killed the child, whereas Jones "merely" let the child die. That is the only difference between them. Did either man behave better, from a moral point of view?
quotes.key_move: Collects the payoff of the paired cases and puts the burden on the reader to find a verdict-changing difference.
quotes.core_assumption: The bare difference between killing and letting die carries no moral weight on its own.
quotes.why_characteristic: The scare quotes around "merely" and the flat closing question are Rachels pressing a distinction until it has to justify itself.

quotes.text: Part of my point is that the process of being "allowed to die" can be relatively slow and painful, whereas being given a lethal injection is relatively quick and painless.
quotes.key_move: States the humaneness argument: the doctrine that permits only the passive option selects the course that produces more suffering.
quotes.core_assumption: Once the decision not to prolong life has been made, the humanitarian motive behind it favors the faster death.
quotes.why_characteristic: Rachels turns the doctrine's own compassionate rationale against it, and does so in plain comparative language rather than principle-talk.

quotes.text: Now, an operation such as that to remove an intestinal obstruction is not prohibitively difficult. The reason why such operations are not performed in these cases is, clearly, that the child has Down's syndrome and the parents and doctor judge that because of that fact it is better for the child to die.
quotes.key_move: Diagnoses what actually decides the infant cases, setting up the charge that the doctrine lets an irrelevant surgical fact determine life and death.
quotes.core_assumption: A doctrine that makes survival hinge on a morally weightless feature of a case is defective, whatever one thinks about the case itself.
quotes.why_characteristic: The Down's syndrome infant cases carry Rachels's second argument, and he presses them without taking a side on the value of those infants' lives.

quotes.text: For example, one may let a patient die by way of not giving medication, just as one may insult someone by way of not shaking his hand. But for any purpose of moral assessment, it is a type of action nonetheless.
quotes.key_move: Dismantles the reply that in passive euthanasia the doctor does nothing, by showing that omissions can be actions.
quotes.core_assumption: Deciding to let a patient die is open to moral appraisal in the same way as deciding to kill him.
quotes.why_characteristic: The handshake analogy is Rachels's way of settling a conceptual point with an everyday case instead of a theory of action.

quotes.text: It is assumed, then, that the parties do not know certain kinds of particular facts. First of all, no one knows his place in society, his class position or social status; nor does he know his fortune in the distribution of natural assets and abilities, his intelligence and strength, and the like.
quotes.key_move: Specifies exactly which facts get deleted inside the choice situation, so that the resulting agreement cannot be shaped by anyone's particular position.
quotes.core_assumption: Knowledge of your class and your natural endowments is morally irrelevant to which principles of justice you should accept.
quotes.why_characteristic: The list of what the parties do not know is the veil of ignorance itself, stated in Rawls's flat inventory style at the opening of §24.

quotes.text: Rather, the guiding idea is that the principles of justice for the basic structure of society are the object of the original agreement. They are the principles that free and rational persons concerned to further their own interests would accept in an initial position of equality
quotes.key_move: Relocates the social contract: the parties agree on principles for the basic structure rather than on entering a society or setting up a government.
quotes.core_assumption: A conception of justice earns its authority from what free and equal persons would agree to, not from tradition, revelation, or an appeal to self-evidence.
quotes.why_characteristic: Rawls announces justice as fairness in this sentence, raising Locke, Rousseau, and Kant to a higher level of abstraction.

quotes.text: It may be expedient but it is not just that some should have less in order that others may prosper.
quotes.key_move: Drives a wedge between an arrangement that pays off in the aggregate and one that can be justified to the person who bears the cost.
quotes.core_assumption: Losses imposed on some cannot be cancelled by gains registered elsewhere in the social ledger.
quotes.why_characteristic: The clipped antithesis of expedient and just is Rawls's sharpest line against utilitarian trade-offs in §3.

quotes.text: In the absence of strong and lasting benevolent impulses, a rational man would not accept a basic structure merely because it maximized the algebraic sum of advantages irrespective of its permanent effects on his own basic rights and interests.
quotes.key_move: Refutes utilitarianism from inside the choice situation by showing that a party protecting his own interests has no reason to consent to it.
quotes.core_assumption: Rational agreement among equals, rather than the size of the total, sets the test a conception of justice must pass.
quotes.why_characteristic: Rawls argues against the principle of utility by asking what a rational party would sign, and the phrase "algebraic sum of advantages" is his.

quotes.text: The two principles mentioned seem to be a fair basis on which those better endowed, or more fortunate in their social position, neither of which we can be said to deserve, could expect the willing cooperation of others
quotes.key_move: Buries the attack on desert in a subordinate clause, then converts it into a demand: the fortunate need terms the badly placed could willingly accept.
quotes.core_assumption: Natural endowment and social starting point are undeserved, so they cannot by themselves ground a claim to greater benefits.
quotes.why_characteristic: The quiet parenthetical denial of desert, attached to an argument about willing cooperation, is a move no other author in the reading makes.

quotes.text: Man is nothing else but that which he makes of himself. That is the first principle of existentialism.
quotes.key_move: States the consequence of existence preceding essence as a flat principle, so that any later appeal to a fixed human nature has already been ruled out.
quotes.core_assumption: No God conceived human beings the way an artisan conceives a paper-knife, so there is no human nature standing behind anyone's conduct.
quotes.why_characteristic: Sartre labels it his first principle in the lecture, and the paper-knife argument that leads up to it is the passage students remember first.

quotes.text: That is what I mean when I say that man is condemned to be free. Condemned, because he did not create himself, yet is nevertheless at liberty, and from the moment that he is thrown into this world he is responsible for everything he does.
quotes.key_move: Defines freedom as a sentence rather than a privilege, joining the absence of any values in an intelligible heaven to total responsibility for what one does.
quotes.core_assumption: With God gone there is no determinism and no justification available, so a person carries the whole weight of his acts without help.
quotes.why_characteristic: The phrase arrives at the end of the abandonment section, right after Sartre quotes Dostoevsky on everything being permitted.

quotes.text: When we say that man chooses himself, we do mean that every one of us must choose himself; but by that we also mean that in choosing for himself he chooses for all men.
quotes.key_move: Answers the charge that existentialism traps a person in private subjectivity by widening each individual choice into legislation for humanity.
quotes.core_assumption: Choosing something affirms its value, and nothing can be better for me unless it is better for everyone, so every act paints an image of man.
quotes.why_characteristic: The claim sets up the worker who joins a Christian union and the man who marries, and it grounds Sartre's account of anguish.

quotes.text: Whereas the existentialist says that the coward makes himself cowardly, the hero makes himself heroic; and that there is always a possibility for the coward to give up cowardice and for the hero to stop being a hero.
quotes.key_move: Rejects the reassurance offered by heredity and temperament, converting a character trait into a deed that the agent keeps performing and could stop performing.
quotes.core_assumption: A temperament is not an action, so nothing about a person's constitution can produce cowardice; only giving way does.
quotes.why_characteristic: Sartre contrasts himself with Zola here and says people are horrified because his coward is guilty of being a coward.

quotes.text: I cannot obtain any truth whatsoever about myself, except through the mediation of another. The other is indispensable to my existence, and equally so to any knowledge I can have of myself.
quotes.key_move: Turns the Cartesian starting point against the accusation of solipsism by finding other people inside the cogito rather than outside it.
quotes.core_assumption: Discovering myself immediately reveals another freedom confronting mine, so self-knowledge runs through a world of inter-subjectivity.
quotes.why_characteristic: Sartre says this while replying to the Communist charge that the cogito cannot reach other people, and he marks the break from Descartes and Kant on the same page.

quotes.text: if I am walking past a shallow pond and see a child drowning in it, I ought to wade in and pull the child out. This will mean getting my clothes muddy, but this is insignificant, while the death of the child would presumably be a very bad thing.
quotes.key_move: Illustrates the preventing-bad-things principle with a case where nobody hesitates, so that the principle is conceded before its cost is revealed.
quotes.core_assumption: A trivial cost to me cannot outweigh a death I am able to prevent.
quotes.why_characteristic: The shallow pond is the example students remember from this article, and it is stated here in Singer's own plain first-person voice.

quotes.text: My next point is this: if it is in our power to prevent something bad from happening, without thereby sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought, morally, to do it.
quotes.key_move: States the single premise that carries the whole argument, pitched to look as uncontroversial as the claim that starvation is bad.
quotes.core_assumption: Obligation attaches to what we can prevent, weighed only against the moral importance of what we would give up.
quotes.why_characteristic: Every later conclusion in the article is derived from this sentence, and Singer repeats it in a qualified form twice more.

quotes.text: If we accept any principle of impartiality, universalizability, equality, or whatever, we cannot discriminate against someone merely because he is far away from us (or we are far away from him).
quotes.key_move: Removes distance as a morally relevant factor by showing that any impartiality requirement already rules it out.
quotes.core_assumption: Physical nearness explains who we tend to help without justifying whom we ought to help.
quotes.why_characteristic: The move from the pond to famine relief depends on this step, and the parenthetical reversal is Singer's own turn of phrase.

quotes.text: It follows from what I have said earlier that we ought to give money away, rather than spend it on clothes which we do not need to keep us warm. To do so is not charitable, or generous.
quotes.key_move: Reclassifies famine relief out of the category of praiseworthy generosity and into the category of what is wrong to omit.
quotes.core_assumption: The line our society draws between duty and charity tracks social convenience rather than moral truth.
quotes.why_characteristic: Singer's attack on the duty/charity distinction runs through spending on clothes, and the flat refusal of the word 'generous' is his.

quotes.text: The strong version, which required us to prevent bad things from happening unless in doing so we would be sacrificing something of comparable moral significance, does seem to require reducing ourselves to the level of marginal utility. I should also say that the strong version seems to me to be the correct one.
quotes.key_move: Admits the most demanding reading of his own principle and endorses it, rather than retreating to the moderate version he used to make the argument easy to accept.
quotes.core_assumption: A conclusion we are reluctant to face counts against our standards of behavior rather than against the argument.
quotes.why_characteristic: The strong/moderate distinction and Singer's willingness to own the harder version appear late in the article and reward a careful reader.

quotes.text: But suppose they were otherwise, what would it avail? The question is not, Can they reason? nor Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?
quotes.key_move: Quotes Bentham to relocate the boundary of moral concern from reason or language to the capacity for suffering.
quotes.core_assumption: What qualifies a being for moral consideration is sentience, not intellect.
quotes.why_characteristic: Singer builds the paper's central argument on this Bentham passage, and the lecture discussion dwelt on it.

quotes.text: Equality is a moral ideal, not a simple assertion of fact. There is no logically compelling reason for assuming that a factual difference in ability between two people justifies any difference in the amount of consideration we give to satisfying their needs and interests.
quotes.key_move: Blocks the move from factual differences in ability to differences in moral consideration.
quotes.core_assumption: Equality is prescriptive; it does not rest on any empirical sameness among beings.
quotes.why_characteristic: The paper's answer to the objection that humans and animals are simply different in fact.

quotes.text: The principle of the equality of human beings is not a description of an alleged actual equality among humans: it is a prescription of how we should treat humans.
quotes.key_move: Reclassifies equality from a factual claim to a prescription, so it can extend past the human case.
quotes.core_assumption: Since equality never depended on capacities, no capacity test can confine it to humans.
quotes.why_characteristic: The hinge of the paper's extension argument, stated in Singer's plainest formula.

quotes.text: The capacity for suffering and enjoying things is a pre-requisite for having interests at all, a condition that must be satisfied before we can speak of interests in any meaningful way.
quotes.key_move: Grounds the sentience criterion: suffering is not one capacity among others but the precondition of having interests.
quotes.core_assumption: Interests, and only interests, generate moral claims.
quotes.why_characteristic: The stone-and-mouse passage that follows this line was the seminar's stock example.

quotes.text: This is why the limit of sentience (using the term as a convenient, if not strictly accurate, shorthand for the capacity to suffer or experience enjoyment or happiness) is the only defensible boundary of concern for the interests of others.
quotes.key_move: Declares every alternative boundary of moral concern arbitrary, leaving sentience as the only defensible line.
quotes.core_assumption: A boundary of moral concern must be principled, and only sentience survives that test.
quotes.why_characteristic: The paper's strongest single claim, with its careful parenthetical hedge on the word 'sentience'.

quotes.text: You should stay and console your friend not because you’ve already met your do-gooding quota, but because it’s your friend that is in distress.
quotes.source_title: Stop the Robot Apocalypse (London Review of Books, 2015)
quotes.key_move: Rejects both the strict and the moderate utilitarian accounts of why you may sit with a grieving friend, and relocates the reason in the relationship itself.
quotes.core_assumption: Personal attachments give reasons directly, without needing to be licensed by a prior calculation of good produced.
quotes.why_characteristic: A student who read the essay will remember the bereaved friend as the case she uses against MacAskill's ledger, and the italicised 'your' as her whole point.

quotes.text: That word ‘arbitrary’ is striking. It is indeed arbitrary that MacAskill went to this hospital and not another, in Ethiopia and not some other country, just as it is arbitrary that we have the family, friends, lovers and neighbours we do.
quotes.source_title: Stop the Robot Apocalypse (London Review of Books, 2015)
quotes.key_move: Concedes MacAskill's premise that his connection to the Ethiopian women was arbitrary, then extends it to every attachment anyone has, so that the premise proves far more than he wants.
quotes.core_assumption: Arbitrary origins do not drain a relationship of moral weight once it is woven into a life.
quotes.why_characteristic: She builds arguments by seizing one word from her opponent — here MacAskill's 'arbitrary' about the Hamlin Fistula Hospital — and turning it over until it breaks.

quotes.text: So it turns out to be better to try to prevent some hypothetical x-risk, even with an extremely remote chance of being able to do so, than to help actual living people.
quotes.source_title: Stop the Robot Apocalypse (London Review of Books, 2015)
quotes.key_move: Follows Bostrom's expected-value reasoning about the astronomical number of future people to a conclusion that its own proponents should find intolerable.
quotes.core_assumption: A calculation that licenses ignoring the living in favour of a vanishingly improbable future benefit has told us something about the calculation, not about our duties.
quotes.why_characteristic: The line delivers the essay's title: the humanitarian arithmetic ends up funding computers rather than bed nets, and the funders are in Silicon Valley.

quotes.text: If everything comes down to the marginal individual, then our ethical ambitions can be safely circumscribed; the philosopher is freed from the burden of trying to understand the mess we’re in, or of proposing an alternative vision of how things could be.
quotes.source_title: Stop the Robot Apocalypse (London Review of Books, 2015)
quotes.key_move: Diagnoses the appeal of individualist moral theory as a form of relief: taking the world as given lets the theorist off the hook for explaining or changing it.
quotes.core_assumption: The proper objects of moral theory include communities, classes and states, so a theory that models only individual choices has narrowed its subject rather than sharpened it.
quotes.why_characteristic: Her closing complaint against effective altruism is political rather than technical, and she ends the essay hoping philosophy has more to give.

quotes.text: But why think this is the right way round? Perhaps it is the universal gaze that cannot withstand our ethical scrutiny.
quotes.source_title: Stop the Robot Apocalypse (London Review of Books, 2015)
quotes.key_move: Reverses the direction of justification between impartial theory and ordinary moral life, so that Sidgwick's point of view of the universe becomes the thing on trial.
quotes.core_assumption: Our own point of view is the unavoidable scene of ethical action, and any standpoint claiming to overrule it owes us an argument.
quotes.why_characteristic: She refuses to let responsibility, kindness and dignity be reimagined to suit a theory, and she puts the question as a challenge rather than a conclusion.

quotes.text: the pain may be no less acute than if he treads on it in contemptuous disregard of my existence or with a malevolent wish to injure me. But I shall generally feel in the second case a kind and degree of resentment that I shall not feel in the first.
quotes.key_move: Holds the physical harm fixed and varies only the attitude behind it, so that the difference in resentment can be traced to the quality of the other person's will.
quotes.core_assumption: Reactive attitudes respond to the goodwill or ill will another person shows us, not to the amount of damage done.
quotes.why_characteristic: The trodden hand is the essay's first homely example, and its conversational 'if someone treads on my hand' register is unmistakably Strawson's.

quotes.text: If your attitude towards someone is wholly objective, then though you may fight him, you cannot quarrel with him, and though you may talk to him, even negotiate with him, you cannot reason with him.
quotes.key_move: Fixes the objective attitude by naming what it makes impossible, marking off quarrelling and reasoning from fighting and negotiating.
quotes.core_assumption: Participation in human relationships and the objective stance towards a person exclude each other.
quotes.why_characteristic: The paired contrasts and the everyday verbs -- fight, quarrel, negotiate, reason -- are the signature of Strawson's account of objectivity.

quotes.text: The existence of the general framework of attitudes itself is something we are given with the fact of human society. As a whole, it neither calls for, nor permits, an external ‘rational’ justification.
quotes.key_move: Blocks the demand for a justification of the moral sentiments by locating that demand outside the framework within which justification operates.
quotes.core_assumption: Justification runs inside the web of human attitudes; the web itself comes with human society rather than resting on an argument.
quotes.why_characteristic: This is the naturalist core of the essay, and the footnote comparing it to Hume on induction makes the move recognizable.

quotes.text: The prevalence of this happy state of affairs would not be a consequence of the reign of universal determinism, but of the reign of universal goodwill.
quotes.key_move: Shows that if determinism entailed that ordinary excuses always applied, what it would really have established is universal good intentions, which no determinist claims.
quotes.core_assumption: Ordinary excuses report facts about intention and circumstance, so no thesis about universal causation can generate them.
quotes.why_characteristic: The dry substitution of 'universal goodwill' for 'universal determinism' is Strawson's wit doing argumentative work.

quotes.text: Sometimes he plugs this gap with an intuition of fittingness – a pitiful intellectualist trinket for a philosopher to wear as a charm against the recognition of his own humanity.
quotes.key_move: Diagnoses the libertarian's appeal to fittingness as a substitute for the moral sentiments he already possesses and refuses to acknowledge.
quotes.core_assumption: The missing element in accounts of desert is the human attitudes themselves, so any metaphysical stand-in for them is superfluous.
quotes.why_characteristic: The 'pitiful intellectualist trinket' line is the essay's most quoted insult and its most concentrated statement of the anti-metaphysical charge.

quotes.text: You wake up in the morning and find yourself back to back in bed with an unconscious violinist. A famous unconscious violinist.
quotes.key_move: Drops the reader into a case built to share the structure of the argument under attack, so that a verdict about the case becomes evidence about the principle.
quotes.core_assumption: Our confident judgments about concrete cases can overturn a general principle that sounded plausible in the abstract.
quotes.why_characteristic: The violinist is the most famous thought experiment in the essay and the sentence students remember first.

quotes.text: suppose it were like this: people-seeds drift about in the air like pollen, and if you open your windows, one may drift in and take root in your carpets or upholstery. You don't want children, so you fix up your windows with fine mesh screens, the very best you can buy.
quotes.key_move: Answers the claim that voluntary intercourse confers a right to the woman's body by inventing a case with the same features, where the intruder plainly acquires no such right.
quotes.core_assumption: Taking reasonable precautions against an outcome is the opposite of assuming responsibility for it.
quotes.why_characteristic: The people-seeds and their mesh screens are the essay's answer to the responsibility argument, and nobody else writes examples like this.

quotes.text: I am sick unto death, and the only thing that will save my life is the touch of Henry Fonda's cool hand on my fevered brow, then all the same, I have no right to be given the touch of Henry Fonda's cool hand on my fevered brow.
quotes.key_move: Refutes the reading of the right to life on which it includes a right to the bare minimum one needs to survive, by finding a minimum nobody has any claim to.
quotes.core_assumption: Needing something for continued life does not by itself give you a right to be given it.
quotes.why_characteristic: The Henry Fonda case is the hinge of her analysis of the right to life, and the cool hand on the fevered brow is unmistakably hers.

quotes.text: By contrast, in most states in this country women are compelled by law to be not merely Minimally Decent Samaritans, but Good Samaritans to unborn persons inside them.
quotes.key_move: Charges her opponents with inconsistency: they demand of pregnant women a standard of sacrifice that no law imposes on anyone else, including the thirty-eight who let Kitty Genovese die.
quotes.core_assumption: Moral and legal demands should apply evenhandedly, so a burden required of one group and no other calls for justification.
quotes.why_characteristic: The Good Samaritan and Minimally Decent Samaritan distinction is her own coinage and does the work of the essay's final third.

quotes.text: So the right to life will not serve the opponents of abortion in the very simple and clear way in which they seem to have thought it would.
quotes.key_move: States the conclusion of the analysis of rights: the premise her opponents rest on cannot carry them to their conclusion without further argument they have not supplied.
quotes.core_assumption: A right to life secures no claim to the use of another person's body, even where that use is needed for life itself.
quotes.why_characteristic: The dry understatement about an argument that fails to serve is her characteristic way of closing a section.

quotes.text: And you are so far off about the just and justice, and the unjust and injustice, that you are unaware that justice and the just are really someone else's good, the advantage of the man who is stronger and rules, and a personal harm to the man who obeys and serves.
quotes.key_move: Recasts justice as a transfer, so that whatever the just man produces by his justice lands in the account of whoever rules him.
quotes.core_assumption: Moral words track the interests of whoever holds power, and obedience is a cost paid by the obedient.
quotes.why_characteristic: The phrase 'someone else's good' is the line every student remembers from the speech that opens against Socrates in the agora.

quotes.text: This, best of men, is what I mean: in every city the same thing is just, the advantage of the established ruling body. It surely is master; so the man who reasons rightly concludes that everywhere justice is the same thing, the advantage of the stronger.
quotes.key_move: Generalizes from the survey of tyrannies, democracies and aristocracies to a single definition covering every constitution.
quotes.core_assumption: Laws are made by rulers for rulers, so the content of justice changes with the regime while its function never does.
quotes.why_characteristic: Only one speaker in Book I defines the just as the advantage of the stronger and dares Socrates to praise him for it.

quotes.text: Because you suppose shepherds or cowherds consider the good of the sheep or the cows and fatten them and take care of them looking to something other than their masters' good and their own
quotes.key_move: Seizes the craft analogy Socrates was using for himself and gives it the reading a herdsman would give it, where care and slaughter come from the same motive.
quotes.core_assumption: Whatever care a ruler shows the ruled is an investment he intends to collect on.
quotes.why_characteristic: It arrives with the taunt about Socrates' wet nurse and his sniveling nose, the rudest moment in the dialogue.

quotes.text: And this must be considered, most simple Socrates: the just man everywhere has less than the unjust man. First, in contracts, when the just man is a partner of the unjust man, you will always find that at the dissolution of the partnership the just man does not have more than the unjust man, but less.
quotes.key_move: Opens a ledger of ordinary transactions, starting with business partnerships, to argue the point from what anyone can watch happening rather than from a definition.
quotes.core_assumption: The question about justice is a question about which life pays, settled by counting what each man ends up holding.
quotes.why_characteristic: The address 'most simple Socrates' and the itemized list running through taxes, distributions and public office belong to one speaker only.

quotes.text: And that is tyranny, which by stealth and force takes away what belongs to others, both what is sacred and profane, private and public, not bit by bit, but all at once.
quotes.key_move: Pushes injustice to its limit case so that the ordinary judgment reverses: the partial thief is reproached, the complete one is called happy and blessed.
quotes.core_assumption: Condemnation of injustice comes from fear of suffering it rather than from any objection to doing it.
quotes.why_characteristic: The escalation from temple robbers and housebreakers up to the tyrant is the climax of the speech he tries to walk away from.

quotes.text: She is willing to bet her life on the latter belief, and in fact does so multiple times daily during her commute. She is not willing to bet her life on the former belief.
quotes.source_title: Fundamentals of Bayesian Epistemology 1: Introducing Credences
quotes.key_move: Uses a difference in what the physicist will stake her life on to expose a difference in doxastic attitude that belief talk cannot register.
quotes.core_assumption: Doxastic attitudes show up in what an agent is willing to do, so any adequate description of them must be fine-grained enough to track betting behavior.
quotes.why_characteristic: The physicist friend, her fusion belief, and her brake pedal are the opening case of the chapter and the example the whole argument for credences is built on.

quotes.text: A fair lottery has sold one million tickets. Because of the poor odds, an agent who has purchased a ticket believes her ticket will not win. She also believes, of each other ticket purchased in the lottery, that it will not win. Nevertheless, she believes that at least one purchased ticket will win.
quotes.source_title: Fundamentals of Bayesian Epistemology 1: Introducing Credences
quotes.key_move: Sets up a set of individually reasonable beliefs that is logically inconsistent, producing a counterexample to Belief Consistency and, via the beliefs about individual tickets, to Belief Closure.
quotes.core_assumption: Rational permission can attach to beliefs that together violate the standard logical norms, so those norms cannot be requirements of rationality.
quotes.why_characteristic: Titelbaum quotes Kyburg's Lottery as the first of the two paradoxes he uses to argue that the natural norms for binary belief are false rather than merely too demanding.

quotes.text: Yet the Simple Binarist—who is willing to attribute only beliefs, disbeliefs, and suspensions—can make out no difference between my friend’s doxastic attitudes toward those propositions. Once the Simple Binarist says my friend believes both propositions, he has said all he has to say.
quotes.source_title: Fundamentals of Bayesian Epistemology 1: Introducing Credences
quotes.key_move: Diagnoses the failure as one of descriptive resources: the binary vocabulary says nothing false, it simply runs out.
quotes.core_assumption: A theory of doxastic attitudes is answerable to descriptive adequacy, and a scheme that cannot state a real difference between two attitudes is thereby deficient.
quotes.why_characteristic: The Simple Binarist is Titelbaum's invented foil, introduced as an illustrative contrast rather than a plausible rival, and he returns to the character throughout the chapter.

quotes.text: Epistemologists sometimes complain that working with numerical credences is unrealistic, because agents “don’t have numbers in their heads”. This is a bit like refusing to measure gas samples with numerical temperature values because molecules don’t fly around with numbers pinned to their backs.
quotes.source_title: Fundamentals of Bayesian Epistemology 1: Introducing Credences
quotes.key_move: Turns aside the psychological realism objection with an analogy, then reframes the real question as whether an agent's attitudes have a structure numbers represent well.
quotes.core_assumption: Numerical credences are representational tools assessed by structural fit, not claims about conscious mental arithmetic.
quotes.why_characteristic: The gas-molecules line is the chapter's most memorable comeback, and it comes right after Titelbaum has listed the genuine costs of numerical representation.

quotes.text: Assigning numerical credences over a set of propositions creates a complete ranking, making it impossible to retain any incommensurabilities among the propositions involved.
quotes.source_title: Fundamentals of Bayesian Epistemology 1: Introducing Credences
quotes.key_move: States a cost of his own framework: numbers force comparability across questions an agent may have no way of comparing, such as election propositions and global warming propositions.
quotes.core_assumption: Representational tools can attribute more structure than the situation contains, and that over-attribution counts against them.
quotes.why_characteristic: Titelbaum argues for credences and then catalogues their disadvantages in the same section, and incommensurability is the cost he presses hardest.

quotes.text: But if there are, I am glad that neither I nor those about whom I care most are among them. By moral saint I mean a person whose every action is as morally good as possible, a person, that is, who is as morally worthy as can be.
quotes.key_move: Fixes the definition of a moral saint and states the reaction the rest of the paper will defend, that one would not want oneself or one's loved ones to be such a person.
quotes.core_assumption: How a life strikes us when we imagine living it, or living near it, counts as evidence about whether it is a good ideal.
quotes.why_characteristic: The paper opens with this admission, and no other author on the syllabus begins by saying he is glad his friends fall short of moral perfection.

quotes.text: A moral saint will have to be very, very nice. It is important that he not be offensive. The worry is that, as a result, he will have to be dull-witted or humorless or bland.
quotes.key_move: Converts the saint's required niceness into a charge about personality, so that the cost of perfection shows up in character rather than in conduct.
quotes.core_assumption: Traits with no moral standing, such as humor and sharpness, are genuine excellences whose absence damages a life.
quotes.why_characteristic: The repeated 'very, very nice' and the deadpan verdict of blandness are Wolf's tone throughout the common-sense section.

quotes.text: For it seems to me that no plausible argument can justify the use of human resources involved in producing a pate de canard en croute against possible alternative beneficent ends to which these resources might be put.
quotes.key_move: Concedes the maximizing argument on its own terms so that the loss of haute cuisine follows from morality rather than from any mistake the saint has made.
quotes.core_assumption: Some activities can be defended only by declining to weigh them against beneficent alternatives, and a saint will never decline that weighing.
quotes.why_characteristic: Wolf argues through specific pleasures, and the duck pate is the example students remember from the gourmet cooking passage.

quotes.text: Despite my conviction that it is as rational and as good for a person to take Katharine Hepburn or Jane Austen as her role model instead of Mother Theresa, it would be absurd to deny that Mother Theresa is a morally better person.
quotes.key_move: Holds two claims together that most theories force apart, granting the saint's moral superiority while denying that this settles whom one should try to be like.
quotes.core_assumption: Moral ranking and the choice of a personal ideal answer to different standards, so the first does not decide the second.
quotes.why_characteristic: Pairing Hepburn and Austen against Mother Theresa is the concrete form Wolf gives to her attack on comparative moral ranking.

quotes.text: Let us call the point of view from which we consider what kinds of lives are good lives, and what kinds of persons it would be good for ourselves and others to be, the point of view of individual perfection.
quotes.key_move: Names a second evaluative standpoint alongside the moral one, giving the paper's earlier complaints a place to stand instead of leaving them as mere preferences.
quotes.core_assumption: Judgments about what kind of person it would be good to be are objective without being moral and without reducing to self-interest.
quotes.why_characteristic: The phrase 'point of view of individual perfection' is Wolf's own coinage in the closing section and marks her positive proposal.

quotes.text: In its new usage, oppression designates the disadvantage and injustice some people suffer not because a tyrannical power coerces them, but because of the everyday practices of a well-intentioned liberal society.
quotes.key_move: Redefines oppression so that the absence of a tyrant no longer settles the question of whether a group is oppressed.
quotes.core_assumption: Ordinary, well-meant institutional practice can produce injustice that no agent intended and no law forbids.
quotes.why_characteristic: The chapter opens by contrasting apartheid and the Hebrews in Egypt with the new left usage, and this sentence is where the switch is made.

quotes.text: Just as everyone knows that the earth goes around the sun, so everyone knows that gay people are promiscuous, that Indians are alcoholics, and that women are good with children. White males, on the other hand, insofar as they escape group marking, can be individuals.
quotes.key_move: Puts three stereotypes beside a piece of settled astronomy to show that they circulate as unremarked common sense, then names who is exempt from being typed at all.
quotes.core_assumption: The dominant group's freedom to appear as individuals rather than as group members is itself an effect of cultural imperialism.
quotes.why_characteristic: The deadpan pairing of heliocentrism with bar-stool prejudice, and the sting in the last clause, are the most quoted lines in the cultural imperialism section.

quotes.text: Marginalization is perhaps the most dangerous form of oppression. A whole category of people is expelled from useful participation in social life and thus potentially subjected to severe material deprivation and even extermination.
quotes.key_move: Ranks marginalization above the other faces by tying expulsion from social participation to its worst historical endpoint.
quotes.core_assumption: Being unusable by the system of labor is a distinct harm, prior to and worse than having too little.
quotes.why_characteristic: Young defines marginals as the people the system of labor cannot or will not use, and this is the judgment she attaches to that definition.

quotes.text: The injustices of exploitation cannot be eliminated by redistribution of goods, for as long as institutionalized practices and structural relations remain unaltered, the process of transfer will re-create an unequal distribution of benefits.
quotes.key_move: Grants that redistribution would correct the pattern, then shows the pattern regenerating because the transfer of energies from one group to another is untouched.
quotes.core_assumption: Justice concerns the social processes that produce a distribution, so a remedy aimed at the outcome leaves the wrong in place.
quotes.why_characteristic: This is the payoff of her reading of Macpherson, Roemer and Reiman, and the clearest statement in the chapter of why she thinks distributive justice is the wrong frame.

quotes.text: The powerless are those who lack authority or power even in this mediated sense, those over whom power is exercised without their exercising it; the powerless are situated so that they must take orders and rarely have the right to give them.
quotes.key_move: Defines a face of oppression by position in the division of labor rather than by any deprivation of goods, singling out those who fall below even the dispersed, mediated power that most people hold over someone.
quotes.core_assumption: The division between those who plan and those who execute is a basic structure of justice, not a mere fact about workplaces.
quotes.why_characteristic: Young introduces powerlessness as the oppression of nonprofessionals alongside exploitation, and defines it negatively against the professional's autonomy, progress and respectability.
